CausalChain: Radiotherapy -> Tumor cell death and neoantigen release -> Activation of STIE and TIME -> Induction of tumor-associated immune regulators -> Upregulation and secretion of Artemin -> Binding of Artemin to GFRα3 on tumor and stromal cells -> Recruitment/activation of suppressive immune cells and cytokine secretion -> Suppression of CD8⁺ T cell activation and infiltration -> Reduced efficacy of PD-1 inhibitor therapy -> Restoration of immune function and improved therapeutic response upon Artemin inhibition
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in NSCLC, radiotherapy-induced cellular stress and tumor cell death lead to a rapid upregulation of Artemin, which, upon binding to its receptor GFRα3 on tumor and stromal cells, orchestrates an immunosuppressive network involving regulatory T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and inhibitory cytokine production. This Artemin-driven loop suppresses CD8⁺ T cell activation and infiltration, thereby limiting the effectiveness of PD-1 blockade therapy. Utilizing advanced CRISPR-based gene editing, selective small molecule inhibitors of Artemin, and real-time in vivo imaging to map spatial and temporal dynamics within the tumor immune microenvironment, we aim to disrupt this loop. The resultant reversal of immunosuppression is expected to synergize with PD-1 checkpoint blockade, ultimately enhancing anti-tumor immunity and therapeutic outcomes.
Abstract: In non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), we propose that radiotherapy not only induces tumor cell death and neoantigen release but also triggers an early upregulation of Artemin, which rapidly engages its receptor GFRα3 on both tumor and stromal cells. This interaction sets in motion a multifaceted immunosuppressive network by recruiting regulatory T cells and myeloid‐derived suppressor cells, as well as by enhancing the secretion of inhibitory cytokines, thereby limiting CD8⁺ T cell infiltration and activation. By leveraging contemporary technologies such as CRISPR-based gene editing, selective small molecule inhibitors, and high-resolution in vivo imaging, our hypothesis posits that targeted inhibition of Artemin signaling can dismantle this immunosuppressive loop in the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) post-radiotherapy. This disruption is anticipated to restore anti-tumor immune competency and synergize with PD-1 checkpoint blockade, ultimately enhancing therapeutic efficacy in NSCLC.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that inhibiting Artemin signaling post-radiotherapy could disrupt an immunosuppressive loop to enhance CD8⁺ T cell responses and PD-1 blockade efficacy in NSCLC. The revised hypothesis builds on this by explicitly detailing the mechanistic steps: radiotherapy triggers not only neoantigen release but also a rapid increase in Artemin expression, which interacts with GFRα3 to recruit suppressive immune cells and inhibit CD8⁺ T cell activity. Additionally, the new version incorporates contemporary technological approaches (CRISPR-based editing, selective inhibitors, and in vivo immune imaging) to facilitate precise modulation and real-time monitoring of the TIME, thus enhancing the practical implementability and empirical testability of the hypothesis.
